title: India's Gold Demand Slips 6% but Spending Hits Record Rs 1.98 Lakh Crore as Prices Soar
excerpt: Indians are buying less gold by weight but spending far more, as record prices reshape consumption patterns and a tariff hike drives a surge in grey-market imports.
body:
• India's total gold demand fell 6% year-on-year to 131.4 tonnes in Q2 2026, but the value of purchases hit a record Rs 1.98 lakh crore — a 50% jump driven by elevated gold prices.
  • Jewellery demand dropped 15% to 75.1 tonnes as consumers shifted to lighter pieces and lower-carat products, while bar and coin investment rose 9% to 50.3 tonnes.
  • Gold ETF inflows surged 49% year-on-year as investors continued seeking alternatives to subdued equity markets.
  • India more than doubled gold import tariffs to 15% in May, which the World Gold Council says has triggered a surge in unofficial grey-market inflows that could exceed 100 tonnes this year.

Indians spent a record Rs 1.98 lakh crore on gold in the April-June quarter even as the volume of purchases fell, the World Gold Council reported on July 30. The divergence captures the central tension in India's gold market: prices have surged so high that consumers are buying less metal but spending far more.

The Volume-Value Split

India's total gold demand declined 6% year-on-year to 131.4 tonnes in Q2, according to the WGC's quarterly report. Jewellery demand fell 15% to 75.1 tonnes — its weakest quarterly showing in recent years outside pandemic-affected periods. Consumers increasingly shifted toward lighter-weight pieces, lower-carat products, and exchange-led purchases as affordability tightened.

Investment demand told the opposite story. Bar and coin purchases rose 9% to 50.3 tonnes, while gold ETF inflows jumped 49% year-on-year to 4.2 tonnes. Gold's appeal as a store of value and a hedge against underwhelming equity returns continued to attract investor capital.

"The arbitrage is so huge. With the 15% duty and 3% GST, there's an 18% difference, and that almost spurs an entire industry."

— Sachin Jain, CEO, World Gold Council India

The Tariff Effect

India more than doubled gold import tariffs to 15% on May 13 in an effort to curb demand, cut the trade deficit, and ease pressure on the rupee. The WGC says the move has backfired in one critical respect: it has triggered a sharp increase in unofficial gold inflows through the grey market.

Indian enforcement agencies seized nearly twice as much gold between May 13 and June 30 as they did in the preceding six weeks, with seizures rising from 86.16 kg to 160.91 kg, according to data the government shared with parliament. Industry officials told Reuters that illegal imports could exceed 100 tonnes this year, up from just 20.4 tonnes in 2025 after duties were previously cut.

Net official gold imports fell 23% year-on-year to 98.1 tonnes in the June quarter — the lowest since the pandemic-hit September 2020 quarter — as the tariff hike redirected demand toward informal channels.

The Global Picture

Globally, total gold demand held broadly unchanged at 1,269 tonnes in Q2, taking first-half demand 2% higher year-on-year to 2,522 tonnes, valued at a record 80 billion. Central banks added a net 289 tonnes to reserves, up 62% from a year earlier. Jewellery demand globally fell 17% year-on-year as high prices weighed on affordability, though spending remained resilient in value terms.

What This Means for NRI Investors

For diaspora investors tracking gold, the picture is nuanced. The WGC projects India's full-year demand at 650-750 tonnes, with the festive and wedding season expected to provide support in the second half. However, elevated prices and a weak monsoon remain headwinds. UBS recently forecast gold reaching ,200 per ounce by mid-2027 — a level that, if reached, would push Indian gold prices even further into record territory.

The structural shift from physical jewellery toward investment vehicles like ETFs and sovereign gold bonds continues to accelerate, offering NRIs more accessible ways to gain exposure without the logistics of physical metal.
